articles.text: At the September 9 school board meeting, Dr. Cheryl Wozniak, Assistant Superintendent, Educational Services gave a presentation on a recent survey to students, parents, and staff regarding distance learning (DL) experiences during the first three weeks of instruction. Some 700 parents, 327 middle and high school students, and 134 staff (paraprofessionals, teachers, and specialists) participated in this survey. Half of the parents reported an overall positive sentiment with another 8% reporting overwhelmingly positive experience with DL. The percentages for staff were similar. However, these numbers were lower for middle and high school students with 36% reporting overall positive, and another 2% overwhelmingly positive experiences. Nearly 4 out of 10 students reported a mixed or overall neutral experience with DL and 5-6% of parents and students reported overwhelmingly negative experiences with DL. Parents were asked more descriptors for DL and nearly a third of parents felt DL was more manageable than they had anticipated, another 22% felt DL was going surprisingly well and another 24% felt DL was challenging but believe it will get better. A significant 22% of parents felt that DL was extremely challenging and unsustainable. Distance learning can be broken down into two major categories, asynchronous learning, and synchronous learning. Synchronous learning refers to students learning together over video calls and asynchronous learning is akin to independent learning using recorded video or homework reading and assignments. Parents were participating in both types of learning with 54% of parents involved in their child’s asynchronous learning most of the time and another 23% involved some of the time. Likewise for synchronous learning, 74% of parents participated most of the time, and another 14% some of the time. Dr. Wozniak reported positive attitudes from elementary school children who are happy to log on and see their teachers and classmates each day. Middle and high school students are reporting better-organized instruction, a more predictable schedule, and learning a lot more than last spring. This is a major win for the school district negotiating with teachers and parents to dramatically improve the experience of distance learning. Families are putting in a lot of time to support their students in distance learning and it is easy to wonder how sustainable this will be going forward. This survey was not meant to measure learning loss compared to previous years; that will take a lot more time and analysis. The district is currently reviewing vendors who test for learning loss. articles.text: A recent report from United Nations University found that nearly 59 million tons of e-waste were generated last year -- that’s 162 times the weight of the Empire State Building. Why is there so much e-waste? A major part of the problem is that when our phones, laptops and other gadgets break, manufacturers such as Apple make it unnecessarily difficult for us to fix them, so we often end up throwing them away and buying new ones. The report found that 59 million tons of e-waste were disposed of worldwide last year -- but only 17.4 percent of that waste was properly recycled. Not only is e-waste the fastest growing type of domestic waste around the globe, but it can be hazardous to our health and can contain toxic chemicals such as mercury. Why should we risk letting these chemicals harm both humans and the environment? We shouldn’t. And we can make California a leader in tackling e-waste by passing right to repair legislation so we can fix our stuff -- not throw it away. Tell your State representative to support consumers’ right to repair. Small electronic equipment, such as iPhones and laptops, made up 5.2 million tons of global e-waste in 2019. Closer to home, U.S. residents discard 416,000 cell phones each day . Yet despite all this waste, manufacturers still make it unnecessarily hard for us to fix our own devices. In 2019, Apple even lobbied against the right to repair legislation. The right to repair gives consumers and businesses access to tools and service information we need to repair electronics and reduce e-waste. Emily Rusch is Executive Director of CALPIRG, a nonprofit advocating for the public interest for healthier, safer lives and cleaner environment.
articles.title: Citizens urged to push state legislators to reduce e-waste

articles.text: Measure UU would allow the City of Piedmont to issue municipal bonds to rebuild the Piedmont Pool. Measure UU is necessary if Piedmont citizens want to have a community pool, as the 56-year-old pool has outlived its viability and soon will be closed permanently. For the past decade, the City Council and staff have taken consistent steps to improve city finances. Apart from our aging infrastructure, which is increasingly expensive to maintain each year, the City stands in a very good financial position. Here are the facts: • Piedmont home sales have not plummeted. The two opponents of Measure UU claim that home sales have plummeted in Piedmont. Not true. During the first months of the pandemic, home sales did contract. However, the number of homes sold has rebounded and returned to levels consistent with prior years. • Measure UU will be paid through property taxes. The two opponents argue that Measure UU will negatively impact the City’s operating funds. Not true. Measure UU would allow the City to issue municipal bonds, which are repaid through property taxes. The bond requirements are totally unrelated to the City’s current taxes and fees. • Long-term pension planning is unrelated to Measure UU. The City has prudently provisioned and planned for the expected annual cost of pension liabilities. Long-term pension liabilities have nothing to do with rebuilding the pool. • The City has no publicly financed debt. The City is expected to receive an AA+ bond rating. Because the City has no publicly financed debt, the bond underwriters are confident the City of Piedmont will receive an AA+ bond rating. The City’s ability to borrow funds in the future will remain strong. It is important to remember that as residents, all of us have benefited from the generosity of prior Piedmont generations who built, paid for, and in many cases donated our beloved public spaces. If Piedmont is going to continue to have a pool for our community and our schools, it is our turn to step up. Instead of searching for misplaced reasons to say no, let’s say Yes to Measure UU, lock in low interest rates, and come together as a community to design, engineer, and build a safe, economical, and sustainable Community Pool for Piedmont for the next 50 years. Bob McBain is Mayor of the City of Piedmont. “We told Dude to shape up or ship out. Unfortunately, he shopped out.”
articles.title: Getting the facts straight on City finances

articles.text: Editor: I couldn’t be more thrilled to support Hilary Cooper in her campaign for Piedmont School Board. Last fall I worked closely with Hilary on the successful campaign to pass Measures G&H. I admire her leadership style, work ethic and organization skills. Hilary has been a strong leader in our community for many years, having been involved in supporting the Piedmont schools including serving as president of both PMS and PHS Parents Clubs, co-chair of Spring Fling and running the Giving Campaign – twice. Hilary’s passion stems from being an educator herself. She was a first-grade teacher in Alamo and a substitute teacher at Piedmont High School. Hilary holds herself to very high standards and I know she would work hard to make our schools the best they can be, especially during these challenging times. France joined the competition for New World discovery in 1524, when King Francis I dispatched Giovanni da Verrazzano to explore the region between Florida and Newfoundland, map the coastline, and find a sea passage across North America to Asia. A violent storm disrupted the journey disabling three of the four-ships in the flotilla. The one surviving ship returned to port, resupplied, and with 50 men, again set sail and made land in two months at present-day Cape Fear, North Carolina. The ship then entered Pamlico Sound, a large lagoon off the coast of North Carolina near the Outer Banks; and in seeking large open water, by the notations in the Captain’s log, the crew believed they had found it and celebrated reaching the South China Sea. Exploration nearly 500 years ago was riddled with miscalculations. articles.text: On the first day of school I encouraged my students, via Zoom, to take this school year one day at a time. Even before I said it, I knew this advice would be hard to swallow. Seriously, how helpful is one day at a time in the midst of the apocalypse, especially to teenagers? But it was the only thing I could think of to say. Why? Because I think it’s true. I think taking this whole situation one day at a time is the only way through it, at least the only way through it while maintaining our sanity. There have been times when I’ve been given this advice myself and felt angry, even offended, because I understood it to mean that I should capitulate. But capitulation is not what I’m suggesting at all. Living one day at a time is not a surrender but rather an acknowledgment, a recognition that some things are out of our control, and that to fight against them heaps even more distress upon our already distressed psyches. But how are we supposed to live one day at a time, when today is so hard? We start with the breath. If you’ve never meditated or considered a mindfulness practice, now is the time to start. I begin my Psychology class each day with a minute of silence. Some students like it, others hate it, some tell me it’s useless, but I’ll keep it up. I know from years of practice that helping students create a habit of paying attention to their breathing and quieting their minds pays huge dividends. After a while, it will start to seem normal to them, even comforting, and then they are on their way to understanding what one day at a time really means. One of the best living proponents of this kind of mindfulness practice is Thich Nhat Hanh, the Vietnamese Zen Buddhist monk. Read any of his books and they will blow you away. At the core of each he exhorts us to pay attention to our breath. That’s it, just breathe. Nhat Hanh’s authority as a teacher, for me, comes from the fact that he found peace in the midst of war. He did not retreat or capitulate or surrender. He breathed his way into the present moment, and there, here, now, he found peace. So that’s it. Just breathe, and pay attention. Nothing more, nothing less, and peace will follow. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.

I enjoy completing the necessary due diligence to understand an issue and its impact on our City. I will always present the facts as I’ve researched them and welcome discussion on any issue with any resident. We have a City of exceptionally bright, critical thinkers, with many experts in a variety of fields. I expect to learn a lot from our interactions. Debates on “controversial items” can become uncomfortable. This is to be expected when people care deeply or feel strongly about an issue. Most important, I will bring all resident feedback to the Council. 2 – No lawn signs. I am respectfully running my campaign differently. Soliciting donations to pay for lawn signs doesn’t make good financial sense to me. It’s a wasteful process. When I ask a resident for money, it will be through our bond measure/ tax process, and because I believe there will be a benefit to them and our City. What benefit do we derive from these campaign signs? None that I can see. Studies show they do not impact a voter’s decision. They are difficult to recycle properly, and visually, they are a blight on our City. My campaign is self-funded. No donations, no lawn signs. As someone who has been in Piedmont for decades, I understand the community’s interests, including the interests of residents who do not currently have children in our schools. I am committed to bringing all of these groups – parents, educators, and the community – together to find the best way forward for our schools. 2 – Extracurriculars, including sports, arts, STEM-related clubs, and a wide array of other activities that our schools and parent groups offer, allow kids to explore and pursue interests that may open up new paths for their lives after graduation. I am committed to working to provide the broadest array of extracurriculars possible so all students can explore their interests. Unfortunately, most of these activities have been cancelled or severely limited by social distancing requirements. I am not a stranger to finding and explaining controversial topics to the public. Moving to extended day kindergarten was the right thing for parents and students but not good for City revenues. I was proud to promote it and I did explain the controversy to the public. Likewise, bond investors were profiting from creative financing that deferred property taxes at the expense of Piedmont taxpayers. I wrote a number of articles about CABs on my website and in the newspaper to explain the issue to the public. I also surveyed readers and over 95% agreed with my assessment. In this election cycle I’ve been writing viewpoints that explain current issues pertaining to the school district. 2 – The coronavirus pandemic has halted extra-curricular activities on school grounds. Sports have been delayed until next semester. The Piedmont pool is shut down, but other pools are open with precautions. Witter Field has been reopened for limited community use. Would the school allow parents to utilize it for track and field, with precautions like social distancing, mask use and not sharing equipment? Infectious disease doctors and epidemiologists have already written to the school district to recommend various precautions for sports and extra-curricular activities. Anything held on school grounds may require a supervising teacher and that requires negotiation with the teachers union. I am not sure the school district is currently in a position to expand outdoor activities even though students need them. Families are having to find alternatives. Some student clubs have moved online. I see many kids biking or walking with their families or social bubbles. The Piedmont Recreation Center currently offers tennis, pickleball, and skatepark activities with precautions. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – During my term on the School Board the past four years, there have been some controversial issues that the Board has had to tackle. At all times, I’ve appreciated the input from Piedmont residents because at the end of the day, one of the most important jobs of a Board member is to represent all stakeholders and make decisions in the best interest of the Piedmont schools. Those who have watched recent Board meetings have seen that I am not afraid to say what I think, even if it might be unpopular. It’s important for the public to know that the only time Board members can discuss ideas all together is publicly at meetings. For those public discussions to be effective, Board members must be direct in their communication, willing to listen and at all times, respectful. 2 – One of the earlier questions asked by the Post was about what students are missing during distance learning. I answered that it is the ability to make in-person connections. During the pandemic, it’s important for students’ social and emotional health that the District help facilitate COVIDsafe activities to create meaning and connectedness. The District has recently opened Witter Field and will be able to use that large outdoor space for “athletic pods” -- small groups of students from our sports teams who will have opportunities for supervised conditioning. Similarly, through our strong partnership with the city, the Rec Department has started to offer “play pods” for our youngest learners. These activities are designed to give our students an opportunity to make in person connections and get outdoors. We need to continue to expand these programs so that students with varied interests can benefit. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: Witter Field reopened for the second time for public use on September 16. The Piedmont School District has announced that Witter Field has reopened for community use as of Wednesday, September 16. This is the second reopening attempt for the city’s largest sports field since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Remaining closed are the baseball and softball fields, batting cages, restrooms at the Field House, Wildwood School lower playground, and access through the Winsor Avenue gate. Access to Witter Field is available from El Cerrito Avenue, the Wildwood Ave. steps, and Piedmont Middle School’s “PE Hill.” Visitors to the field must wear face coverings, keep six-foot social distance from others who are not part of the same household, and stay home when sick with a fever, cough, or other COVID-19 symptoms. “The District previously closed Witter Field due to widespread and persistent lack of compliance with the Alameda County order at the Field, and similar issues led the City of Piedmont to close the Linda Beach Playfield, as noncompliance poses a serious public health risk,” wrote the district in a press release. Staff photo Witter Field initially closed at the beginning of Alameda County’s Shelter-in-Place orders on March 17. When the county restrictions were eased on June 9, Witter Field reopened. The field was closed a second time on August 3 and remained closed until last week. The school district’s press release also states, “Witter Field is an important community resource and the decision to reopen the facility was made based on supportive public input. The Field will remain open as long as users comply with the public health orders issued by Alameda County.”
articles.title: Witter Field reopening given another chance

articles.text: Tadej Pogačar, a 22-year old Slovenian with UEA Team Emirates, pulled off a monumental upset over fellow countryman Primoz Roglič of Jumbo-Visma by overcoming a 57-second deficit in the Stage 20 time trial to win the yellow jersey and one day later be crowned on the ChampsÉlysées in Paris as winner of the 2020 Tour de France. Pogačar became the only cyclist in history to win the yellow jersey, the white jersey as best young rider, and polka-dot jersey as best mountain climber. He is also the youngest rider to win since 1904. “It’s unbelievable. It’s really crazy,” Pogačar said, via Cycling News. “Even if I didn’t win, even if I came second or last, it’s nice to be here. This is the top of the top. I cannot describe this feeling with words.” One week ago, Pogačar trailed Roglič by 40 seconds after the 16 Stage mountains. He improved his lead to 57 seconds in Stage 17. That lead remained until the race’s penultimate stage, a time trial one day before the race ends each year on the streets of Paris. The time trial was a short 36.2-kilometer course from Lure to La Planche des Belles Filles on Saturday, September 19. With a lead of just shy of one minute, the easy expectation was that Roglič could not lost that amount of time on a short course and would be assured of winning the Tour. But Pogačar beat all the predictions and expectations by Photos courtesy of CyclingNews.com Tadej Pogačar (middle) shocked the world with a dramatic Stage 20 comeback to win the Tour de France. Countryman Primoz Roglič (left) placed second and Richie Porte finished third. clocking a time of 55 minutes and 55 seconds. He finished 1 minute, 21 seconds ahead of second-place stage-finisher Tom Dumuolin and, more incredibly, 1:56 ahead of Roglič, who placed fifth in the time trial. In the dramatic race, Pogačar had gained 13 seconds by the first checkpoint at 14.4 km, while Roglič seemed to begin to fall apart at the start of the initial climb, appearing fatigued and quickly losing ground. Roglič relinquished 36 seconds at the start of the climbing section and did not show the resilience he exhibited during the five mountain Stages, 15-19. Pogačar flew up the final climb 22 seconds faster than any other rider, a first category mountain, at a grade of 8.3 percent at 6 km in length. Roglič was still 20 seconds ahead at the start of the climb, but dramatically lost 1 minute, 22 seconds by the final checkpoint with 2.7 km remaining. Pogačar was beside himself with emotion at the end of Stage 20; crediting his team for training and preparing him for every turn of this year’s Tour. “I think I’m dreaming. I don’t know what to say. It’s unbelievable,” said the champion at the end of the Stage 20 time trial. “My dream was just to be on the Tour de France [podium],and now the dream is true. I’m here and now there’s only the last stage. This is unbelievable. I’m really proud of the team. “They [teammates] did such a big effort. To get the yellow jersey on the final day is what we dreamed from the start. We did a reconnaissance and I knew every corner, every pothole in the road, I knew when to accelerate and that’s congrats to all the team. I pushed to the end and I made it,” he continued. Tadej Pogačar stormed up the final mountain in Stage 20 to seal his victory. Primoz Roglic held the yellow jersey until Stage 20. He is shown visibly rattled as he climbs up the final mountain. Tadej Pogačar breaks down with tears after winning Stage 20 and the yellow jersey of the 2020 Tour de France.
articles.title: Tadej Pogačar shocks world, wins Tour de France with dramatic Stage 20 finish

articles.text: The second week of the National Football League has come and gone with nearly everything going as expected. The Las Vegas Raiders pulled off a big 34-24 upset of the New Orleans Saints in their opening of Allegiant Stadium in Vegas, and the San Francisco 49ers posted an easy 31-13 win over the Jets, but suffered five costly injuries. The Raiders are now 2-0 and 49ers are 1-1. We wrote last week that Jon Gruden’s Raiders defense could shift its focus to running back Alvin Kamara and receiver Emmanuel Sanders in order to secure a victory with their AllPro receiver Michael Thomas out. Sanders was held to just one reception. Vegas heads to New England to play the Patriots and QB Cam Newton in Week 3. It’s harder to envision an upset this time, given that the Pats have one of the best defenses in the league. SF 49ers As the only remaining NFL team in the Bay Area, the 49ers walked out of New York with a win but with extensive injuries: defensive linemen Nick Bosa and Solomon Thomas, running backs Raheem Mostert and Tevin Coleman, and quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo. It’s a string of injuries that would leave many teams throwing in the towel on the season, especially in the ultra-competitive NFC West. But the 49ers have one of the best coaching staffs in the league with head coach Kyle Shanahan and defensive coordinator Robert Saleh. So, no time to panic. The next three weeks may determine whether the 49ers can remain in the race for the NFC West. Even without the injured players, SF is favored against the Giants in Week 3 and have meetings set with the winless Eagles and Dolphins in Weeks 4 and 5. So, the 49ers could be 4-1 with players returning by their Week 6 divisional game against the Rams. So don’t panic yet, Niners’ fans. Oakland A’s clinch AL West The compressed 60-game regular season is coming to a close. Those Swingin’ A’s have clinched first place in the American League West for the first time since 2013. It marks their third consecutive trip to the playoffs. The A’s are still in the mix for one of the top two seeds. If the season ended today Oakland would play the sixth-ranked Houston Astros. The SF Giants are a half game back of a final wildcard spot. SF has done itself no favors by losing three of their last four games. They are finishing up a series with the Colorado Rockies and have a final four games with the Padres, a must-win series. The Roots play tomorrow against Detroit City, with a final group match against Michigan Stars on Sunday, September 27. Recently promoted to the United Soccer League, the Rootes look to win Oakland’s first professional soccer championship since the Oakland Clippers won the NPSL in 1967. articles.text: Staff Photos Look for this sign to start your trail at Harkins Ridge. Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve is a historic park in the MidPeninsula Open Space Preserve. Pictured here is Purisima Creek. Another view of Purisima Creek, where remnants of old logging mills from the early 1900s still exist. The Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve of San Mateo County is a part of the Mid-Peninsula Open Space Preserve. It is known for its towering redwood trees, wildflowers, ferns, and views of the rolling mountains south toward Big Basin. Purisima Creek was closed for several weeks after the nearby fire at Big Basin State Park clouded the air with smoke. It had been a few weeks since our last hike due to continued poor air quality, so the forecast on Sunday for clear skies was visibly refreshing. According to the Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve website, the coastal redwoods throughout Purisima Creek are second-growth, likely around 100 years old. Many large stumps, 10 to 20 feet in diameter, are visible in the park. The Preserve includes over 24 miles of developed trails, going down to the Purisima Creek Trail – an old logging path – up to peaks with gradients above 15 degrees. Sunday’s hike was a 6.7-mile loop along the Harkins Ridge Trail to Whitemore Gulch Trail, and then back to the parking lot. Starting at Harkins Ridge you go downhill about 230 feet for the first 3.5 miles. You pass beneath groves of redwoods and get a brief glimpse of Purisima Creek. After the creek and a right-turn through a gate, you begin to gain over 300 feet in less than a half mile, and then another 450 feet in the next mile. The final two miles of the trail back to the parking lot includes over 900 feet in elevation gain, including seven switchbacks that rise nearly 400 feet over the course of a mile. In total, this hike included over 1,600 feet in elevation gain. Although several sites list as Sometimes described as “heavily trafficked trails,” the trails on Harkins Ridge and Whittemore Gulch averaged only seven people per mile on my hike. For directions, enter Purisima Creek North Ridge Trailhead to access this loop. Nearby is the South Parking Lot, which connects you to the historic Purisima Creek Trail. The trail will take you beneath second-growth redwood trees and vast amounts of ferns native to the region. Several switchback turns provide hikers with a good workout from consistent elevation gains. Portions of the hike are in open, sunny areas. Some picturesque trees and trails of Purisima Creek’s Whittemore Gulch trail. A view of the rolling hills in San Mateo County.

It had been a few weeks since our last hike due to continued poor air quality, so the forecast on Sunday for clear skies was visibly refreshing. According to the Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve website, the coastal redwoods throughout Purisima Creek are second-growth, likely around 100 years old. Many large stumps, 10 to 20 feet in diameter, are visible in the park. The Preserve includes over 24 miles of developed trails, going down to the Purisima Creek Trail – an old logging path – up to peaks with gradients above 15 degrees. Sunday’s hike was a 6.7-mile loop along the Harkins Ridge Trail to Whitemore Gulch Trail, and then back to the parking lot. Starting at Harkins Ridge you go downhill about 230 feet for the first 3.5 miles. You pass beneath groves of redwoods and get a brief glimpse of Purisima Creek. After the creek and a right-turn through a gate, you begin to gain over 300 feet in less than a half mile, and then another 450 feet in the next mile. The final two miles of the trail back to the parking lot includes over 900 feet in elevation gain, including seven switchbacks that rise nearly 400 feet over the course of a mile. In total, this hike included over 1,600 feet in elevation gain. Although several sites list as Sometimes described as “heavily trafficked trails,” the trails on Harkins Ridge and Whittemore Gulch averaged only seven people per mile on my hike. For directions, enter Purisima Creek North Ridge Trailhead to access this loop. Nearby is the South Parking Lot, which connects you to the historic Purisima Creek Trail. The trail will take you beneath second-growth redwood trees and vast amounts of ferns native to the region. Several switchback turns provide hikers with a good workout from consistent elevation gains. Portions of the hike are in open, sunny areas. While delivering his final sermon last week, McNabb estimated that he had preached about 760 sermons in Piedmont. His legacy as Senior Minister expands well beyond Piedmont. He has maintained a lasting sister-church relationship with Imani Community Church, an African American congregation in Oakland, providing a link between the two communities. Under his tenure and with the hiring of Rev. Scott Kail as Youth Minister in 2002, Piedmont Community Church vastly expanded its commitment to build homes outside Tijuana, Mexico for impoverished families. During that time, hundreds of homes have been built by Piedmont teens and adults. McNabb’s outreach efforts have even crossed continents into Malawi, Africa, where a sister church relationship continues to blossom. Rev. Dr. Don Ashburn, the Associate Minister in Piedmont, noted that McNabb made a real difference in the world, the church and the community. He praised McNabb for opening up the Piedmont community to its neighbors near and far. “In a time when our lives are in a constant state of flux, it’s good to know we can continue to build on the solid foundation of ministry and mission he’s helped to lay. When he arrived nearly two decades ago, Piedmont Community Church — if it was known for anything at all outside of Piedmont — was seen as a close, but also somewhat closed, community. Bill did a whole lot to open us up.” “I’ll miss him as a colleague of 17 years, but I’m glad to continue calling him my friend,” Ashburn said. Building homes in Mexico a Rite of Passage The church-sponsored trip to Mexico during Spring Break each year has become a rite of passage for Piedmont’s youth. The legendary trip began in the 1970s with just a single van of teenagers bound for an orphanage across the Mexican border. Last year more than 300 people spent a week on the outskirts of Tecate. Those who volunteer to go to Mexico are equipped with the necessities only – hand tools and the basic building supplies to raise permanent homes for up to 16 families in one week. McNabb at t r ibutes the expanded interest in the program to the church’s youth minister, Rev. Scott Kail. “Shortly after I arrived here, I was asked to find the best youth minister in the country,” McNabb said with a smile. “We were told that Scott Kail was who we should pursue. It took me six months or so to talk Scott Kail into coming all the way from Long island, but we were able to move him and his family to Piedmont.” Before Kail came, the Mexico trip did not expand much from the single van of volunteers, McNabb recalled; but a year ago, 320 youth volunteers traveled across the border to help build homes. It was the largest volunteer house-building group there. It is so popular among Piedmont teens, there is a waiting list for placement. Last year, it sold out in about 14 seconds. McNabb noted that it changes people’s lives year after year. Students return home with new perspectives and a deep reflection of their own privileges. In turn, Kail recognized McNabb’s accomplishments in relation to youth ministry and charitable works. “Bill McNabb’s time as Senior Pastor of Piedmont Community Church was full of so many programs and ministries that helped the poor and those in need. In his tenure, over 300 homes were built,” Kail confirmed. A bridge to Malawi McNabb, along with members and friends of the Piedmont Community Church, established a close, permanent bond to a thriving Christian community in Malawi, Africa. Over the years, McNabb frequently visited Kafita Presbyterian Church, now Piedmont’s official sister church in Lllongwe, Malawi, fostering a bridge See Rev. The construction of the sanctuary was made possible by the Better World Fund, and money raised from parishioners in Piedmont. McNabb said that he already had a pre-existing relationship with the Presbyterian hospitals in Malawi. “I flew over there in 1986 with Maureen to look for a mission hospital to support as part of our Capital Campaign at Miami Shores. We were going to give away 20 percent of what we were going to raise in that campaign,” he said. His church in Miami Shores donated an ambulance, but couldn’t get anyone to deliver it past Zimbabwe. Undeterred, McNabb flew to Zimbabwe with three friends and drove the ambulance about 1000 miles to Malawi. “It was one of the most incredible experiences of my life,” he said with a broad smile. McNabb’s most recent trip to Africa was in June 2019. Now inspired by the success of the outreach to Africa, the church has recently expanded its efforts to explore supporting missions in South America. Branching out to the East Bay Under McNabb’s leadership, Piedmont Community Church has formed a sister church relationships with Imani Community Church in Oakland. A chance meeting of two pastors, McNabb and Rev. Dr. George Cummings, forged a close bond between their churches. “It was after we had such positive experience with Kafita in Malawi that we tried to find a sister church closer to home,” McNabb said. McNabb started going to the Pastors of Oakland breakfast once a week to find a church that aligns with Piedmont Community Church’s mission and inclusivity. “All of a sudden, George [Cummings] got up to speak, and I knew he was different. This was an educated person who was very progressive. When he spoke, I knew that I found ‘him’,” McNabb recalled. McNabb invited Cummings to lunch, and then for dinner, finding many similarities between them – they even shared the same birthday. Through that friendship, a sister church relationship was born. Piedmont Community Church continues to raise funds for ongoing programs in Oakland and Berkeley – focusing on homelessness and food insecurity. Reflections on retirement McNabb’s beginnings in Piedmont were overshadowed by the tragic events of 9/11. His first Sunday preaching from the pulpit in Piedmont was September 9, 2001, two days before the terrorist attack on New York City and Washington, DC. And now his retirement comes upon the heels of a global pandemic, and his last sermon was delivered to an empty room. Still, McNabb reflects joyfully on the past 19 years, his beginnings, and his retirement. “It was an interesting way to start and end a ministry. We were in this together, we were going to get through it,” McNabb said. He offered similar sentiments throughout the public health crisis – in the form of short, shared video messages. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir offers three departments for its 200 young singers: the Kinder Department, Training department, and Performing Department. The Kinder Department is comprised of students ages 4 through 6 in two different sets: the pre-kinder choir (ages 4-5 and in preschool), and kinder choir (ages 5 – 6 and in kindergarten). Both offer a child’s first exposure to choral music in a friendly, nurturing, and playful environment. “It’s really their first exposure to music,” said Artistic Director Eric Tuan. “We offer something that’s developmentally appropriate, like singing together, and introducing folk songs and musical games that will later be used in the training department to derive melodic patterns,” Each class in the Kinder Department meets weekly for fifty minutes. Pre-kinder choir sections are limited to 10 students, and kinder choir sections are limited to 12. Each class offers a “Family and Friends Recital” at the end of each semester. The youngest department is led by Anne Daniel, now in her fifth year, who oversees PreKinder Choir, Kinder Choir, and Girls Training 1. “She’s just terrific – with the little ones in particular,” Tuan said. Immersing students at this age in choral music has many benefits. Tuan noted the social development that comes with working in tandem. At age four and five, children begin noticing rhythmic patterns and are able to mimic them. In preschool and daycare, singing can help children improve their capacity for learning. Singing together in a choral setting is one of the first community-building exercises that a child will experience. Piedmont Children’s Choir offers teaching methods that are closely linked to the developmental stages of the growing mind, and a choir is the perfect opportunity for a young child to learn to navigate a social group in a shared activity with a common goal. “There really isn’t competition in the choir, only cooperation,” Tuan explained. “If your weakest singer does better, the whole group does better. There is a connectivity.” Most students who graduate from the kinder department continue on to the training and then performing group. The goal for many children is to be in a performing group that travels outside the state and county for summer choral competitions. Part 3 in the series will explore the training department. articles.text: Musaics of the Bay’s “Stayat-home Symposium” is a virtual community collaboration and series of broadcasts featuring music premieres based on both music and art. It is a collaboration among composers, performers, artists of all types. Last week’s symposium featured violinist Maya Buchanan performing the music of composer Elise Arancio, whose work, “Wherever I Go, You Go,” was inspired by a painting entitled “Vision Unfolding” by Tim Petrin and an accompanying poem by E.E Cummings. The poem, I Carry Your Heart With Me, was a common theme throughout the broadcast. Arancio introduced the poem. “I feel like this poem is especially powerful, and this time, while so many people are separated by physical distance, it’s a great reminder that we carry the people that we love close to us no matter the circumstance,” Arancio said. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré RBG are the initials of Ruth Bader Ginsberg, until her death on Friday this week a sitting judge on the U.S. Supreme Court. The three letters are also the title of a well-crafted documentary about a remarkable woman who, to paraphrase both Martin Luther King and Barack Obama, has time and again proven in her legal career that “The arc of a moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.” RBG in essence is a civil rights film about the pernicious effects of gender discrimination. It was Ginsberg who early in her career as an attorney decided that if it was possible to bend the arc of history toward equality for women (and men), whatever the context, then she might be able to accomplish such profound change inside of a courtroom as an advocate and later from as a judge. The arc for Ginsburg has indeed been long, beginning when she was very young. Her intellect was always present; however, her restraint, her deliberative personality, absent anger or resentment, reflects the repeated counsel of her mother, who died when Ginsburg was only 17. After law school at Harvard and Colombia, slowly and tenaciously, and despite her diminutive stature and quiet, decorous manner, she argued case after case, each buttressed by well-reasoned points of view. The film opens with a montage of anti-Ginsburg voices, each taking exception to her advocacy for equality regardless of gender. The language spoken is vitriolic and unexpected. One example is when Ginsburg stepped forward to argue that there was no legal basis for Virginia Military Institute refusing to enroll qualified women. She won, and women eagerly matriculated to VMI. It was classic RBG – not her first victory nor would it be her last. Ruth Baker Ginsberg, subject of the documentary RBG. The film seamlessly merges Ginsburg’s unparalleled work habits with her personal life, most especially her love for her husband, Martin Ginsburg, a successful New York tax attorney. Together their marriage and two children were deeply valued. While Ginsburg was reserved and focused, her husband y was easy-going and jocular. They created a charming balance, creating a much-envied harmony that lasted for decades. The film shows that while RBG had an ability to focus on the law and its historical precedents, it was when she was nominated by Bill Clinton to the Supreme Court, in 1993, that she became, ever so gradually, a judicial rock star. What caused her surprising almost pop culture fame was that the court’s pendulum was slowly swinging toward conservatism. As a result, Ginsburg found herself often penning sharp and eloquent dissents, documents that were closely read and which took an important place in the decisions of the court. Ginsburg has become an iconic symbol for feminists across the nation, her image and her initials in conjunction with the word “notorious,” referencing, tongue in cheek, rapper “Notorious B.I.G.” Hence the recent biography, titled Notorious RBG. As a film, RBG is a valentine to this remarkable woman who has, using the language of the law, spoken in courtrooms large and small and by doing so, has changed the landscape of America. Her journey has been astonishing, born of iron spine and will. And it still continues. It was suggested to her that after two bouts with cancer during Obama’s tenure she might consider retiring, allowing him to nominate a younger justice. She explained that she was committed to serving as long as she was able. And able she was until her death this week on September 18, 2020. RBG. Documentary. Directed by Betsy West and Julie Cohen. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. This review was originally printed in the Piedmont Post on May 20, 2018. articles.text: A violin made by F.O. Stanley in 1908. The piedmont Fourth of July parade is famous. There are the Oompa-Loompas and the great Piedmont Community Band. But the classic cars are viewed with excitement. I am always fascinated by the Stanley Steamers. They remain the classics of classic cars. But these classics were only a passing interest of the Stanley brothers. One of their passions will outlive the steamers by hundreds of years. If you ever need inspiration, look to the Stanley brothers. Long before cars even made an appearance on the scene, the Stanley brothers were successful. F.O. and F.E. Stanley were twins and used their initials as their names. They began their first business in an elementary school. It was some type of a maple syrup business, and it was a success. Their next success was to develop an x-ray focusing mechanism. Shortly after this, they invented a new photographic process. They sold it to George Eastman who sold it to the public as Kodak. Eastman made a fortune and so did the Stanleys. This was the seed money to start manufacturing the famous cars. Everyone knows about the Stanley Steamers. But what few may remembeer is that the best steam car ever made was made in nearby Emeryville. Moving ahead a few years, FE Stanley was killed in a traffic accident and FO Stanley came down with tuberculosis. Seeking to recover his health, he moved to Colorado. Not only did he love Colorado, but he regained his health. He invested his money wisely and went into the hotel business. The Stanley Hotel in Estes Park, Colorado remains a destination and houses the Stanley museum. But the brothers’ real interest superseded even fame and money. All those things – the cars, the x-ray machine, the photographic process, the hotel business – they all came later. The first thing the young Stanley boys learned will outlive everything else that they did. Their uncle, who had the colorful name of Liberty Stanley, was one of the first American-born violin makers. How he got his colorful name is another story. He was born in 1776, and the boys made their first violin at the age of 10. Later when they acquired a real Stradivarius violin, they took notice of the wood that Stradivarius used. They bought wood from the same forest as the great Stradivarius himself. Not only did they use it for their own violins, they used it in their Stanley Steamer cars. FE Stanley became great friends with Henry Ford. But it wasn’t their love of automobiles that cemented the friendship. No, it was their love of violins. Henry Ford bought two violins made by Stanley to accompany the two Stradivarius violins that he owned. While all those other things may be seen as passing fancies, the Stanley violins should last at least 500 years. I was said that a Stanley Steemer never needed a tuneup. But a violin? Now that’s another story. Good news It seems that good news is on the horizon. The Dallas Symphony has resumed with live concerts. They presented an all-Beethoven concert recently, and all precautions were observed. The 36 musicians on stage wore masks. The audience, which normally numbers 2000, was limited to 79. Needless to say they were very enthusiastic. The critics were happy to report that the small orchestra played with great clarity and enthusiasm. It is a start back to normalcy, and is indeed good news. F.O. Stanley

He is encouraged to begin a journey west and try and discover what the source of the disturbance is. He rides a Yakkuru, a beast that is part horse, part antelope and part goat. He finally arrives in an area prowled by Moro (Gillian Anderson), a hybrid wolf that is also part God. It is then that he sees for the first time a young woman named San (Claire Danes), also known as Princess Mononoke (a mononoke is a spirit of a beast). San is a human child, raised as a wolf, and rides a spirit wolf. And so the story continues, a panoramic trip with extraordinary characters and places, reflecting the deep imagination of Miyazaki. It’s a multilayered, richly told story. But know that it is one of Studio Ghibli’s darkest animated films and may not be suitable for the little guys. While it is mythical history, it also engages, using action and melodrama, which for older audiences will enthrall; it never approaches anything like graphic violence. The artistry is magical and masterful, qualities that define all of the films of Hayao Miyazaki. Princess Mononoke (1999). Animé by Studio Ghibli. Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Billy Crudup, Claire Danes, Gillian Anderson and Minnie Driver. 2 hrs., 13 min. articles.text: Walking through town, it becomes clear to me that two things stand out as chief characteristics of the architecture in Piedmont. The first is the individuality of the homes — virtually all of the homes are “one-off” designs, built before the advent of seemingly ubiquitous tract homes. Today, even in many expensive new communities, because of economy of scale, developers often build the same home in large groups, robbing the place of the rich character, individuality and texture of the streets and community that we see here. The second observation is the high quality of design and construction throughout the city. Part of the pre-tract home era in which Piedmont was started, also included noted individual architects for each house. We benefited from (and continue to benefit from) the talents and expertise of an era of excellent local architects, including Julia Morgan, Albert Farr, Miller Warneke, and W.H. Weeks. This valuable contribution continues today with top designers and architects such as Mark Becker, Glen Jarvis, and John Malick to name just a few. And with top designers seems to come a higher level of craftsmanship which results in buildings that not only look better, but last for generations. What most people immediately think of when reference is made to architecture, is the exterior appearance of a building. As we will see in this series, although the exterior shape, form or style is only part of what can be considered good architecture, it is of course very important. It is important not only for the owners, but also for the many people experiencing it: guests, neighbors and passers-by. A building and its visual relationship to adjoining buildings and landscapes (its context) necessarily is a part of and helps form the entire community. This is why building height, Well designed doors, windows, hardware and light fixtures are all among the many important details that make up the overall architectural character and quality of buildings. articles.text: Due to the Labor Day holiday on the first Monday of September, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had their Zoom book discussion on September 14.. With the recent death of Congressman John Lewis and society’s current focus on racial and social justice, the group decided to read Lewis’ Across That Bridge. There was a solid turnout of 14 members of the group for the call. Participating were Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Alicia Rivera, Jeri Lockhart, Laura Goldman, Adrienne Hamlin, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Margie Blodgett, Pat McSwain, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. John Lewis was a civil rights pioneer and icon. He was one of the leaders of the 1963 March on Washington and a speaker with Martin Luther King Jr. at the Lincoln Memorial. In 1965, Lewis led a march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, an event which became known as “Bloody Sunday.” State troopers and police attacked the marchers, leaving Lewis and others battered and bloody. Lewis later served 17 terms in the U.S. House of Representatives representing Georgia from 1987 until his death earlier this year. During this time he was a champion of civil rights and social justice. He was also the author of seven books, including Across That Bridge, drawing from his personal experiences as a civil rights leader to offer guidance on the importance of living a virtuous life and how to change the world without the use of violence. The reading group universally enjoyed Across That Bridge. Lewis followed his Christian faith and Gandhi’s principles of non-violence to accomplish change. The readers felt Lewis’ themes of love and non-violence are timeless and inspiring. The group discussed how the debate between violence and non-violence for achieving change continues. It was questioned how much the current generation knows about the power of non-violence today. The readers agreed that there has been racial progress in our country, but that we still have a long way to go, and that violence makes situations worse. It can be discouraging to see that change is not as rapid as many would like. People become impatient, but the process of change is like a relay race where the struggle is passed from one generation to the next. The group’s hope was that it will not take another hundred years to achieve true racial justice in our country. Lewis provided insights from his actions in the ‘60s which the readers felt can be used to bring change now. The group felt that this is a book for the next generation of leaders, as it reads like a guide on how to conduct themselves and accomplish change. Faith in God and Lewis’ cause kept him going on a personal level and motivated him in peaceful resistance. The group agreed Lewis was a great man, that Across That Bridge is a fine book, that it had generated a group conversation by the reading group, and that discussions are importaant even though the issues are uncomfortable. The outpouring of love for John Lewis at his death was understandable for the readers. Laura Goldman noted that actor Morgan Freeman read Lewis’s final words at his funeral. They were words that Lewis wrote at the very end of his life, Alicia Rivera had recently listened to this remarkable oratory (available at https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=_i2DSkAys-8), and hoped others would listen to it as well. Alicia commented that America lost a true leader during our troubled times. In dicussing future books to read and discuss, the group selected Caste by Isabel Wilkerson for November and Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austin for December. They earlier made The Dutch House, a novel by Ann Patchett, their October selection. The group has read mostly recently written books, and thought reading a classic like Pride and Prejudice would be an interesting change. The group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, October 5, at 1:30 p.m. New members are welcome, and there is no fee to participate. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Dryden Once again, the bicycle team Linda and Marvin will be riding in memory of Linda Lettieri and Marvin Stern, both of whom passed away from ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, better known as Lou Gehrig¹s Disease). July 9 marked the 13th anniversary of Linda¹s passing and the 15th year our bicycle team, Team Linda and Marvin, will be participating in the Ride to Defeat ALS. This is truly a science fiction-like disease in its progressive reduction of your ability to move, speak and eventually, breathe. Since ALS is currently not well understood, has no cure or effective treatment path, we are working hard to fund-raise to find a cure through the ALS Association, Golden West Chapter. Finally, there are some glimmers of hope that some of the genetics of ALS are being discovered, although we are a long way from effective treatments and the eventual cure. The ALS Association is the only non-profit organization fighting Lou Gehrig’s Disease on every front. By leading the way in global research, providing assistance for people with ALS through a nationwide network of chapters, coordinating multidisciplinary care through certified clinical care centers, and fostering government partnerships, The Association builds hope and enhances quality of life while aggressively searching for new treatments and a cure. Team Linda and Marvin will be riding this Saturday, September 26, in their memory and we are soliciting your support to help our team exceed our fundraising goal for ALS research. Last year, through the amazingly generous donations of friends, family, and clients, we raised over $70,000 for ALS Research. The timeline for a cure or even a treatment for ALS may be very long, and we may not be around long enough to see it, but the goal is worthy of our effort and hopefully your dollars. Any contribution, no matter how small (or large!) will be appreciated and will help fund research into the causes and cures of ALS. Your tax-deductible gift will make a difference in the lives of many! It is faster and easier than ever to support this great cause. A skate park subcommittee, initially comprised of Recreation Commission members Vincent Fischer, Carrie Graham Lee, and Glyn Burge, Rec. Department staff members John Wilk, surveyed the skate park last year and made recommendations on some improvements. “The subcommittee, in May 2019, came to the commission and gave their recommendations. The purpose of that committee was to review current skating and scootering options in the city, and explore ways to offer more skating opportunities,” Putzer said. Putzer also noted that the skate park is suitable only for intermediate skaters and older, information acknowledged by the subcommittee. Some recommendations pointed to a potential redesign in order to make it a better fit for the community. “[The subcommittee] wanted to make it a better fit for beginner-to-intermediate skaters, give it some space, give it shade and maybe a place to picnic,” she said. The commission approved those recommendations last year, Kennelly Skate Park is behind Coaches Field and the Piedmont Corporation Yard. but the recommendations never were formally approved by the council. “Now it’s in a bit of a holding pattern,” Putzer said. The subcommittee has since disbanded, but the recommendations still wait for council approval. Commission Chair Steve Roland noted that the subcommittee provided great insight on improvements to the park last year, but their report ultimately fell to the wayside due to COVID-19. “Eventually, the [recreation] commission passed it on to city council, and it was out of our hands. That led right up into the pandemic, and here we are,” he said. A Coaches Field master plan, currently under CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act) review, can potentially incorporate some of the intended designs for the Kennelly Skate Park. This would include a possible picnic area, as well as other design aspects that were suggested. The recommendations will probably go to council for approval at a later date, Putzer explained. The Recreation Department is currently using the skate park as a temporary preschool area, as indoor daycare services remain shuddered due to COVID-19.

articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont pool has been enjoyed by generations and continuing do so is an understandable goal for Piedmont. The proposed ballot measure is not a very appropriate or responsible way for Piedmont to meet that goal. 1. The Piedmont City Council recently identified two capital improvement projects for consideration. The first project was upgrading the public facilities (police, fire and city offices) to meet “essential services” requirements to assure that they function during a natural disaster. The estimated cost was $30,000,000. The second project was a new community pool. Based on early program descriptions and no actual design documents, the estimated cost was $15,000,000. 2. Clearly the function of city services after a natural disaster would seem to be the first priority in the implementation of these projects. 3. Instead, the Piedmont City Council put a $19,000,000 bond issue on the ballot to fund a community pool, even though that same council put the estimated cost of the project at $15,000,000. 4. This project is described as a community pool. Historically, and in the promotional materials, Piedmont School District sports programs and swim classes are identified as using the facility, thus limiting community use without remuneration. Incidentally and historically, over the last 40 years at least, the School District has refused to request that Piedmont citizens fund a school pool. 5. The vaguely suggested scope of the project goes way beyond the existing facility. It seems to be tailored for water sports not community use. The specter of swim meets looms with the attendant parking nightmare. 6. A complete rehabilitation of the existing facility that would replace all piping and equipment, seal and refinish the existing pools, is certainly worth exploring, and would absolutely cost far 7. By putting the pool project ahead of public safety and putting a measure on the ballot with insufficient definition of scope of work is, to put it charitably, a mistake. Piedmont is a very small town with very limited bonding capacity and the pool is just not a first priority. We can have our pool, but not this way. Please vote no. There is time and there another way. –Alan Rudy, AIA
articles.title: A new pool? Take time and do the job right

articles.text: Editor: I am writing in support of Measure UU, the local bond measure which will provide the funds necessary to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable new pool facility for the entire Piedmont Community. There is little dispute that the current pool has reached the end of its useful life. Despite repeated attempts by prior City Councils and community members to secure a new aquatics facility, no significant work has been undertaken to replace this critical 56-year-old community resource. I urge you to join me in supporting the decision of our bright, diligent, elected officials who have thoughtfully placed this measure on the ballot now, after significant research and consultation. Be assured, that an independent Citizen Bond Measure Oversight Committee will monitor the prudent use of all funds raised. East Bay voters had the foresight to approve the formation of the East Bay Regional Park District during the depression. Let’s emerge from this Covid cloud with the promise of a sparkling new pool facility open to all Piedmont families, students, and seniors. Please join me in voting YES on Measure UU. –Cathy Michelotti Glazier

articles.text: Editor: In troubling times like these, it is more important than ever to elect a strong, committed, and capable leader who will work towards the common good of all, not just a few. We wholeheartedly endorse Conna McCarthy for Piedmont City Council because she has shown these qualities over her years of valuable service to the Piedmont community. We have known Conna for over 15 years and have admired her leadership on key Piedmont committees, commissions, and school boards. She tirelessly led critical initiatives on the Parent boards of both Piedmont Middle and Piedmont High School. Also, she was influential on the Parcel Tax Committees, advocating for our children and residents. In addition to championing for schools, she has worked hard as the Vice Chair of the Recreation Commission and Chair of the CIP Committee making recommendations on capital expenditures on City facilities. We have witnessed Conna being whip-smart and dedicated but also collaborative and compassionate. Conna and her thoughtful leadership will have a strong, positive impact on our town. We hope you’ll join us in voting for her on November 3 for City Council. –Debbie and Dan Lee
articles.title: McCarthy – working toward common good of all

articles.text: Editor: During this difficult time in our history, we need leadership to unite, think creatively and act for the benefit of the entire Piedmont community, especially students and teachers. As a candidate for school board, Hilary Cooper fits that bill with her vast, multi-dimensional experience as classroom teacher, volunteer and fundraiser. As president of parents’ clubs, she exhibited her ability to collaborate with different viewpoints, a much-needed skill for a school board member. With my background as a Havens teacher, parent and grandparent of Piedmont students, I see the need for an experienced individual to help the success of our schools by being able to juggle the various needs of students, teachers, administration and parents. A vote for Hilary is a vote for success for the entire community. –Elene Manolis
articles.title: Cooper able to collaborate with differing viewpoints

articles.text: Editor: I have gotten to know Cory Smegal from working together on the Wildwood Site Council and on Health & Safety preparedness, and from watching her in numerous School Board meetings. Cory is an exceptional board member. She actively listens to parents and educators, does her homework and researches best practices. Cory is a clear thinker who asks direct questions and advocates for what’s in the best interest of students. As a pediatrician, I am concerned about the health and well-being of all our students, especially now. Cory consistently ensures that the board prioritizes student mental health. She doesn’t just talk about what’s needed, she actively explores how to solve problems. Recently she’s been talking about how to find ways for students to make meaningful in-person connections while in distance learning. Cory has advocated to bring students back to the classroom as soon as it’s safely possible, starting with those who have the most difficult time with distance learning and those who pose the least risk in terms of spreading SARS-CoV-2. Cory has worked hard to secure the financial health of our District. She has led local fundraising efforts such as the Giving Campaign, actively campaigned to pass school bond measures, and advocated alongside administrators, teachers and parents for better state funding. As Board Correspondent, Cory has improved communication by making a point to respond promptly and thoughtfully to the countless emails sent to the board over the past two years. At this time of unprecedented challenges, we need experienced leaders. Cory is the current Board Vice-President and if re-elected, she is next in line to be Board President in December. Please join me in re-electing Cory to the School Board. More than ever, we need her leadership. –James E. CrawfordJakubiak, MD
articles.title: Smegal an exceptional School Board member

articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont Planning Department will soon begin updating its housing and zoning policies, known as the “Housing Element,” as part of a periodic process required by state law. Given the close connection between housing and racial segregation, this process is an opportunity to put substance behind the City Council’s recently passed Resolution Unequivocally Rejecting Racism. Piedmont’s population is 92% White and Asian, in stark contrast to the rich diversity of the surrounding region. Piedmont’s homogeneity was caused by historical practices like redlining, racial steering, deed restrictions, and explicit racial discrimination. The story of Sidney Dearing, Piedmont’s first African American homeowner, is illustrative: Dearing purchased a home in Piedmont in 1924. Bombs were found at his home on three occasions. At one point 500 neighbors gathered and protested on his lawn. Piedmont’s police chief at the time – a KKK klansman – refused to protect the family. Eventually Dearing was forced to sell his home to the City. (For more details see www.sidneydearing.com.) Such egregious practices were outlawed by the 1968 Fair Housing Act. Yet racial segregation persists. Today, one of the primary means of preserving racial homogeneity is exclusionary zoning – laws that mandate that a city’s housing consist mainly of single-family houses. Like many other predominantly white suburbs, Piedmont historically has fought to preserve its single-family zoning (which comprise 98% of the city’s housing) and to keep out dwelling types that would draw more diverse residents. In contrast, the city of Minneapolis abolished single-family zoning in 2019 and now allows up to three units on most lots. The state of Oregon recently passed a law permitting duplexes throughout the state. Piedmont should follow these examples and embrace varied and affordable forms of housing – including duplexes, triplexes, and multi-family dwellings – that will open our community to more diverse residents, while maintaining the small-town qualities that many appreciate. As a city, we have too long been governed by an ethos of preserving the status quo and allowed discussions of “neighborhood character,” “property values,” and “parking” to function as code words for upholding exclusion. As our nation grapples with the legacy of racism, we must back up our words with actions to create a more integrated and just community. We invite community members interested in the link between housing policy and racial equity to join us for a Zoom panel discussion on September 24, organized by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign with PADC and the League of Women Voters. This year’s Harvest Festival, originally scheduled for Piedmont Park this Sunday, September 27, will take place but as a virtual celebration due to restrictions brought on by the pandemic. “As disappointing as not having an in-person event is, the city recognizes that the most important thing right now is to keep the community safe and healthy,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “Because of the nature of the Harvest Festival, social distancing measures would not be possible to achieve, let alone enforce, during this event,” This year’s Festival featured a photo contest and a youth coloring, drawing, and collage contest. The Recreation Department encouraged Piedmont residents to share harvest gardening successes with the virtual festival. Residents emailed photos of their home-grown edibles, preserves and cooking at one photo per category. The deadline for photo submissions was Friday, September 18. Categories for submissions include: tomato, pumpkin, squash, jam, bread, mustard, best cookie, dried fruit and veggie, salsa, unusual fruit, curds and butters, jam, apple pie, cake, cucumber pickles, ugly edible, honey, preserved edible, “other” pie, pesto and sauce, preserved veggie, and compost pile. The youth coloring contest was sponsored by the Piedmont Tamisha Apodaca’s honey. Susan Hill’s biggest tomato weighs over 1 pound. Garden Club, and kids ages 14 and younger were able to download a poster, create their own vegetable drawing or make a collage from the nature scavenger hunt page found on the recreation department’s website. [This] is essentially a way to engage all the ages as we’re all sheltering in place,” said Susan Hill, founder of the Harvest Festival. She added that designing the festival virtually allows for a wider breadth of possibilities. “We look forward to getting back to the normal harvest festival next year. It’s quite a tradition in Piedmont,” Recreation Commission Chair Steve Roland said. To view more submissions, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/cms/ one.aspx?portalId=13659823&pa geId=17046963.
